theme: Paul arrested; his defense in the Temple
readingInstruction: Read Acts 21:1-22:30. Paul goes up to Jerusalem despite warnings, is seized in the temple, and gives his testimony from the steps of the barracks. Notice his courage, and how he retells his conversion.
settingTheScene: Paul has finished his third journey and reaches Jerusalem around AD 57, with gifts for the poor believers. Prophets warn him in city after city that chains await. He goes anyway. In Jerusalem, rumors have spread that he teaches Jews to abandon Moses. The leaders suggest that he demonstrate his faithfulness by joining a vow in the temple. It leads to his arrest and the long imprisonment that takes him to Rome.
observation: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (21:13).
“And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, Let the will of the Lord be done” (21:14).
“Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place” (21:28).
“I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city” (21:39).
“Brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day” (22:3).
“And I answered, Who are you, Lord? And he said to me, I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting” (22:8).
“And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name” (22:16).
“Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles” (22:21).
interpretation:
On the way, Paul and his companions stop in Tyre, where disciples urge him through the Spirit not to go to Jerusalem. In Caesarea, the prophet Agabus takes Paul’s belt, binds his own hands and feet, and says that the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt. His friends beg him not to go. Paul replies with a moving statement: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” When he would not be dissuaded, they said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” He is not reckless. He is obedient.

In Jerusalem, James and the elders rejoice at the reports of the Gentiles. But they tell Paul that thousands of Jewish believers are zealous for the law and have heard that he teaches Jews to forsake Moses. They suggest he pay the expenses of four men under a vow. Paul agrees, an example of his flexibility (1 Corinthians 9:20). But Jews from Asia see him in the temple, seize him, and cry out that he has brought Greeks into the temple and defiled it. The whole city is stirred up. They drag him out and beat him, and he is rescued by the Roman tribune and his soldiers, who bind him with two chains.

As he is carried up the steps, Paul asks the tribune, in Greek, for permission to speak. The tribune is surprised. Paul addresses the crowd in Aramaic. He tells his story: a Jew born in Tarsus, trained under Gamaliel, zealous for God, who persecuted the Way to the death. On the Damascus road, he met the risen Jesus. Ananias said: “The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash your sins away, calling on his name.” Then Paul tells of a vision in the temple, where Jesus said, “Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.”

At the word “Gentiles,” the crowd erupts, shouting, “Away with such a fellow from the earth!” The tribune orders him brought into the barracks to be examined by flogging. Paul asks the centurion, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?” The tribune becomes afraid. The next day he brings Paul before the council. Once again, Paul’s Roman citizenship protects him.
connection: Acts 9:1-19 and 26:9-18 are the other accounts of his conversion. Galatians 1:13-16 gives his own testimony. Philippians 3:4-11 lists his Jewish credentials and counts them as loss. 1 Corinthians 9:19-23 describes his adaptability. Luke 9:51 shows Jesus setting his face toward Jerusalem. Romans 15:25-31 is Paul’s request for prayer about the trip. 2 Corinthians 11:23-28 lists his sufferings. Matthew 26:39 is Jesus’ prayer, “Not as I will, but as you will.”
application:
Practice telling your own story of how you met Jesus in two minutes.

Ask whether there is a step of obedience you have avoided because of fear.

Pray “Let the will of the Lord be done” for a situation you cannot control.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you courage to obey even when it costs you.
Thank Jesus for setting his face toward Jerusalem.
Ask him to make you a witness in your setting.
